newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Falco Biosystems eyes tie-ups, mergers. [corrected 11:35 gmt]
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Falco Biosystems eyes tie-ups, mergers. [corrected 11:35 gmt]

text.p: Japan's Falco Biosystems Co Ltd, which conducts clinical tests for hospitals, said it will seek more business tie-ups or mergers with smaller rivals at a time when the industry, facing a tougher environment, is poised for drastic restructuring.

Falco Biosystems president Hiroharu Akazawa told Reuters in a recent interview that greater competition in the clinical inspection business would force smaller rivals whose annual sales are less than one billion yen to restructure further or seek partners to merge with.
The president said his company would actively seek mergers and weather competition by scale, but did not specify any likely counterparty candidates.
Only weeks after listing its shares on the Osaka and Kyoto bourses on April 18, the company acquired 71.4 percent of the shares of a unit of Daiichi Clinical Laboratories Inc.
(Corrects to make clear that it acquired a unit of Daiichi Clinical, not Daiichi itself)

Falco, based in Kyoto in western Japan, has recently expanded business into areas such as carrying out health checks for corporate employees and food security inspections, which has seen growing demand after a killer food poisoning epidemic swept the nation last summer.

Akazawa saw business booming in the food inspection-related business, saying his company's sales in that area would increase to 800 million yen in the year to September 1998, from current annual sales of around 200 million yen.

"I would like to bring annual sales (in the food inspection-related business) to 1.5 billion yen, accounting for about 10 percent of our total sales in the future," Akazawa said. He did not give a specific target year.

"The second pillar of (our business) would be health checks for company employees. We would like to bring annual sales in this sector to 1.5 billion yen from the current 700 million yen in the future."
For the current year to September 1997, the company last month predicted a current profit of 1.27 billion yen, after the previous year's actual profit of 950 million yen.
Akazawa said he saw current profit rising to 1.7 billion yen in 1997/98, and 2.3 billion in 1999/2000.
